item.title: How Owning vs. Renting Impacts Your Psychology and Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

How Owning vs. Renting Impacts Your Psychology and Happiness

Here's what the research says about how our housing shapes our happiness.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Homeowners are more satisfied with their housing, but not necessarily with their lives.
  • Stressful mortgage debt can offset the well-being benefits of owning a home.
  • Housing instability, rather than renting itself, is most consistently linked to worse mental health.

Homeownership is part of the American dream and, for some, a rite of passage into adulthood. Over the last five years, we have seen a stagnant housing market due to a variety of factors, including a lack of supply, stubbornly high mortgage rates, and generally increased prices of buying a house and all of the associated costs that come along with it. Due to the current market, people are renting at higher rates than have been previously seen in prior generations, with the median age of a first-time homeowner listed at 40 in 2026 in the United States (National Association of Realtors 2025).

Are Homeowners Happier?

The answer is more complicated than you might expect. Homeowners do report being more satisfied with their homes than renters, and that satisfaction lasts. One long-term study in Germany found that people who move into a home they own like their housing more, with little fading even after five years (Clark & Diaz-Serrano, 2021). But feeling good about your house doesn’t necessarily translate into feeling good about your life. Another German study that followed people over time found that buying a home raised housing satisfaction but had no lasting effect on overall life satisfaction (Will & Renz, 2024).

Much of the answer comes down to money. In that same study, the mortgage was the culprit. The cost of paying off a home loan lowered life satisfaction enough to cancel out the benefits of owning. A separate study using data from the U.S., U.K., and Australia found that the “owners are happier” gap comes mostly from people who own their homes outright. Homeowners with a mortgage and little equity saw much of that happiness advantage disappear (Clark et al., 2025).

Overall, the findings on happiness are mixed. The picture gets clearer when we look at other parts of our psychology.

How Owning Impacts Your Psychology

A poll of over 10,000 adults in the U.K. found that 40 percent of renters reported feeling lonely, compared with 29 percent of people who own their homes outright. Renters were also much less likely to know their neighbors (43 percent vs. 69 percent) and less likely to be satisfied with their friendships (Belonging Forum, 2024). However, renters tend to be younger, earn less, and move more often, and each of these could contribute to loneliness on its own since this report was a simple poll.

Renting may even show up in our biology. In a study of about 1,400 adults in the U.K., people who rented privately looked biologically older than homeowners, based on patterns of DNA methylation, a marker of aging at the cellular level. The size of the effect was surprising: renting was associated with nearly twice the aging effect of being unemployed (vs. employed), and 50 percent more than having been a smoker (vs. never smoking) (Clair et al., 2023). The study was observational, so it can’t show that renting causes faster aging.

What might explain these patterns? A review of 22 studies of renters offers a clue. Housing instability, such as frequent moves or the threat of eviction, was linked to worse mental health in 12 of the 14 studies that looked at it. High rent was linked to worse mental health in six of nine (Talmatzky et al.). Renting itself may be less of a problem than the insecurity that often comes with it.

The Bottom Line

Homeownership is associated with several psychological benefits, including greater satisfaction with one’s home, stronger ties to neighbors, and less loneliness. It also seems to improve overall well-being when the mortgage is manageable, or the home is paid off. Owning may also become part of who we are. Research on car sharing found that people who shared cars instead of owning them felt less connected to the cars and less responsible for them (Bardhi & Eckhardt, 2012). Homes may work the same way.

But the research suggests that much of what makes owning feel good is stability: knowing you can stay, putting down roots, and not worrying about next year’s rent. That’s good news for renters. When you can, stay in one place longer, get to know your neighbors, and invest in your community. These choices may give you many of the psychological benefits usually credited to owning a home.

Although sometimes more expensive on a monthly basis than renting, paying off a mortgage can operate as a critical savings mechanism for people because the money put toward the home leads to owning the home outright and providing a valuable asset to the owner. Ultimately, the decision to buy versus rent has become complicated for younger generations. Most importantly, doing meaningful work, staying healthy, and having an excellent social life with friends and family are much more important determinants of living a good life than your choice to rent or buy.

item.title: Fried to a Crisp: Why Seasonal Workers Burn Out
item.description:
Burnout

Fried to a Crisp: Why Seasonal Workers Burn Out

Why seasonal work is uniquely stressful and what can help during the off-season.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Many seasonal workers struggle with burnout due to the high-demand, high-intensity nature of their work.
  • Transitioning from an all-consuming schedule to the off season can feel like psychological whiplash.
  • Burnout can include irritability, exhaustion, apathy, restlessness, and feeling directionless.
  • Patience, easing back into routines, and reorienting to what matters most can help ease symptoms of burnout.

Here it is, the day you’ve been waiting for. You get to sleep in your own bed, wake up without a 3 a.m. alarm, and bask in the glorious silence of a quiet house.

And yet, you feel agitated and restless, tossing and turning all night despite feeling completely depleted. You feel flat and down instead of how you think you should feel (grateful and happy). You have been looking forward to this moment all summer, but now that it’s arrived, you just feel apathetic.

Why Do Seasonal Workers Struggle With Burnout?

Seasonal workers face a unique pattern of work-related stress. This is especially true for those whose work intensifies during the summer season, such as mountain guides, outdoor educators, park rangers, wildland firefighters, and hospitality workers, among others.

High intensity, high demands.

Seasonal work can consume enormous amounts of physical, mental, and emotional energy. Instead of working a predictable eight-hour workday with established breaks, many seasonal workers may be working multiple days straight. There may be long hours, early mornings, minimal sleep, and very little time or energy left over for other parts of life.

High responsibility and risk.

Some seasonal employees work in high-stakes environments in which they are directly responsible for the welfare of other people. Making complex decisions in high-risk situations can be equally exhilarating and exhausting.

What can be fun is also stressful.

Seasonal work can involve relocation, travel, and a constantly changing environment. While seasonal work may appeal to people who enjoy these aspects of novelty and adventure, they can simultaneously be stressors in themselves. It can be hard to maintain routines around self-care, sleep, and other parts of life with an unpredictable schedule. After a few months, this can take its toll.

Financial anxiety.

Seasonal work often comes with a time stamp, which can kick anxiety around finances into overdrive. You may find yourself struggling with questions of what’s next even before the season ends.

While burnout can look different from person to person, symptoms can include:

  • Exhaustion
  • Sleep disturbance (difficulty falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much)
  • Irritability (having an especially short fuse)
  • Feeling overwhelmed by everyday decisions
  • Loss of interest in activities typically enjoyed
  • Social isolation
  • Feeling numb, flat, or mentally checked out
  • Feeling restless and directionless

Controlling the Burn

Thankfully, there are many things that can help ease the intensity of seasonal work-related burnout.

Be gentle with yourself and embrace the transitional period.

Patience and self-compassion are critical in the early phases of transitioning out of the season. It can feel like psychological whiplash to go from a high-intensity, high-risk work environment to a completely open schedule. Putting pressure on yourself to jump immediately back into productivity can have a paradoxical effect—not only will you feel more stressed, but the anxiety may actually get in the way of productivity.

What is needed here is time. Your brain is working in overdrive to integrate the intense experiences you just had and adjust to a new pace of life. If your schedule allows, take the opportunity to rest and gently ease back into routines. Do more of whatever fills your cup, whether that is time with friends, finding solitude in nature, or traveling someplace totally different.

The key here is to notice when you are putting pressure on yourself to feel a certain way, and to instead meet these thoughts and emotions with understanding and kindness.

Rebuild Routines and Structure.

While a true break may be necessary for mental decompression following an intense season, eventually it will be time to get back on track with habits and routines. When many parts of life have been “on hold” for months, it can feel overwhelming to know where to begin.

Make a list for yourself of all the things you both need to do and want to do. Identify 2-3 priorities for the next week. Then, make an action plan: What are the actual steps involved with getting started? The more that you can break these down into small, manageable pieces, the more likely you will be to follow through.

Tackling goals one step at a time eases the feeling of overwhelm, while also creating necessary momentum for the next chapter.

Reconnect With What Matters.

Rest and recovery can help recharge spent batteries at the end of a long season, but it’s equally important to consider how you want to spend your time once you have more of it.

Values are compass points that give our lives direction and meaning. These compass points can shift and change alongside life experiences, stressors, and traumas. Your values may be different today than they were at the start of the season.

Ask yourself: “What matters most to me right now outside of work?” It could be spending more quality time with loved ones and less time on your phone, giving back to your community, taking care of your physical body, or reconnecting with spirituality.

Know When to Reach Out for Help.

For symptoms of burnout that continue to escalate to the point that they get in the way of daily life, impact relationships, or cause significant distress, consider reaching out for support from a mental health professional. Therapy modalities such as acceptance and commitment therapy or cognitive behavioral therapy are effective for treating stress, anxiety, depression, trauma, and other concerns. Some individuals find benefit from medication management as well.

With careful intention, you can help transition burnout from "fried to a crisp" to "warm bread."
Source: Ellie Burgin / Pexels

Conclusion

Emerging from a long, difficult season is a big adjustment. Given the high-intensity, high-demand, high-risk nature of many types of seasonal work, it is understandable why many workers wrap up the season feeling burnt to a crisp.

Just as your body needs time to recover after intense exertion, so too does your mind. You can facilitate psychological recovery by meeting yourself with compassion and patience, easing back into routines and habits, and reorienting yourself to what matters most in this new chapter.

Little by little, these efforts can take you from “burnt” to “toasty” and, eventually, “just warm bread.”
